docs.title: Processing
docs.text: Processors transform Document objects between parsing and splitting (and again after splitting, for split-local enrichment). Each one is a small, universal operation — because elements carry their visual properties as inline CSS, the same processor works on output from every parser.

docs.title: The contract
docs.text:
Every processor subclasses DocumentProcessor and implements one method:

class MyProcessor(DocumentProcessor):
    async def process(self, document: Document) -> Document | None:
        ...
  • Async-only — pure-sync processors simply don't await anything.
  • Return None to drop the document. ProcessingPipeline short-circuits on None (later processors never run), IngestPipeline.run() returns None, and DocumentPipeline.run() returns [] chunks for the filtered file. In the sync pipelines, direct-mode VectorStorePipeline and MentionStorePipeline treat a filtered source as "yields nothing" and delete its stale stored entries, while DocumentStorePipeline skips it with a warning and keeps the stored Document.
  • Extend metadata, never replace it. Write individual keys (document.metadata["x"] = ...); assigning a new dict silently discards filename and everything earlier processors wrote. Library-written metadata keys are for external consumers only — no processor may read or branch on them.

Chain processors with ProcessingPipeline, or just pass a list to the pipeline — IngestPipeline(processors=[...]) accepts either:

from ragdoc.pipeline import DocumentPipeline, TokenSplitter
from ragdoc.processing import HeadingLevelProcessor, TitleDetectionProcessor

pipeline = DocumentPipeline(
    processors=[HeadingLevelProcessor(), TitleDetectionProcessor()],
    splitter=TokenSplitter(max_tokens=4000),
)

docs.title: Structure (no LLM)
docs.text: Processor What it does HeadingLevelProcessor Re-derives heading levels from visual properties (font size, bold, centered, all-caps) via a pluggable SizeToLevelMapper TitleDetectionProcessor Promotes the most title-like heading to document.title FootnoteProcessor Detects footnote markers and links them to their definitions via a pluggable FootnoteResolver (SimpleFootnoteResolver is heuristic; LLMFootnoteResolver breaks ties with an LLM) EmptyDocumentFilter Returns None for documents with no meaningful content — the canonical drop-a-document example DocumentDumpProcessor Side-effect processor: serializes each passing document to disk (debugging / audit trails), returns it unchanged

docs.title: LLM-based enrichment
docs.text:
Processor What it does LLMHeadingResolver Sends heading candidates to an LLM for semantic level assignment (document-title / h1–h6 / none) — for documents whose visual styling is inconsistent ImageSummaryProcessor Writes an LLM description into each Image.text_representation, which render_for_prompt uses as the text fallback; construct with ImageSummaryProcessor(summarize=openai_image_summarizer(client)) DocumentSummarizerProcessor Writes a whole-document LLM summary to document.metadata["summary"] (recursive fold for documents beyond the token budget); idempotent unless overwrite=True

LLM processors need the llm extra (pip install 'ragdoc[llm]').

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
Order matters — later processors see the output of earlier ones. The natural sequence:

  1. Heading structure first (HeadingLevelProcessor, then LLMHeadingResolver if needed) — splitting and title detection both depend on correct levels.
  2. TitleDetectionProcessor — after levels are trustworthy.
  3. FootnoteProcessor — once structure is stable.
  4. Filters last (EmptyDocumentFilter) — drop documents only after enrichment had its chance; anything after a filter never runs for dropped documents.

docs.title: Pre-split vs post-split placement
docs.text:
Processors passed to IngestPipeline run once per document, before splitting — right for whole-document concerns (headings, title, footnotes, filtering).

Split-local enrichment (e.g. summarizing each retrieval unit rather than the whole file) runs after splitting: splits are still Document objects, so the same processor classes work. Run the stages yourself when you need this:

from ragdoc.splitting import split_document

doc = await ingest.run(path)                     # parse + process (pre-split)
splits = split_document(doc, renderer, tokenizer)

summarizer = DocumentSummarizerProcessor()       # writes metadata["summary"] per split
# (requires a configured LLM client — raises LLMNotConfiguredError at construction otherwise)
enriched = [await summarizer.process(s) for s in splits]

chunker = SimpleChunker()                        # then chunk each enriched split
chunks = [c for s in enriched if s is not None for c in await chunker.chunk(s)]

docs.title: Configuring the LLM
docs.text:
DocumentSummarizerProcessor, LLMFootnoteResolver and the default ImageSummaryProcessor() resolve their client through one chain (see the LLM API): an explicit client wins (client=; for ImageSummaryProcessor the summarize= callable you build from a client), else the openai_client of the active RagdocConfig (set with configure(...)), else construction fails loudly with LLMNotConfiguredError. RagdocConfig.openai_client accepts any client with a chat and/or an embeddings attribute (ChatClient | EmbeddingsClient; an AsyncOpenAI has both). Processors need the chat capability, so an embeddings-only client there also raises LLMNotConfiguredError. LLMHeadingResolver has its own chain — explicit client=, then a client built from LLMHeadingResolverSettings (base URL + API key), then the config client — and raises ValueError when none of them yields a chat-capable client. configure() is a context manager — the config is active inside the block:

from openai import AsyncOpenAI
from ragdoc import RagdocConfig, configure
from ragdoc.processing import DocumentSummarizerProcessor

async with configure(RagdocConfig(openai_client=AsyncOpenAI(), default_llm_model="gpt-4.1")):
    summarizer = DocumentSummarizerProcessor()   # resolves the client from the active config
    document = await summarizer.process(document)

Every call goes through the shared reliability layer (ragdoc.llm): one retry policy (429/connection/timeout/5xx with jittered exponential backoff) and structured parsing with explicit refusal errors. Three things worth knowing:

  • Retry-After is capped. A Retry-After header on a 429 replaces the computed delay, but never beyond backoff_max (30 s by default) — a server asking for an hour does not park the pipeline for an hour.
  • One retry layer. For a real AsyncOpenAI / AsyncAzureOpenAI client the library calls through client.with_options(max_retries=0), so the SDK's own retries do not stack under ragdoc's: a call makes exactly max_retries + 1 HTTP attempts, and the max_retries you set on the client itself is ignored for ragdoc calls. A custom client object is called as is.
  • Timeouts. Each LLM processor has a per-request timeout knob (request_timeout, in seconds: LLMHeadingResolverSettings, DocumentSummarizerSettings, openai_image_summarizer(...), LLMFootnoteResolver(...)). The default None sends no per-request timeout, so the client's own timeout applies.

Degrade semantics are per-processor by design: the heading resolver returns no changes on failure, the image summarizer skips the failing image with a warning (any LLM-call failure — a refusal, a 400 for one bad image, exhausted retries; programming errors and cancellation still propagate) and continues with the next image, the footnote resolver leaves the footnote unresolved, and the summarizer raises.

LLMHeadingResolver resolves heading levels even when the document already has a title; in that case the model's document-title judgment is ignored and the two title-removal options (remove_title_from_elements, remove_elements_before_title) do nothing. LLMHeadingResolver additionally supports env-based client configuration via LLMHeadingResolverSettings (LLM_HEADING_RESOLVER_API_KEY, base URL, model).

docs.title: Writing your own processor
docs.text:
from ragdoc.document import Document
from ragdoc.processing import DocumentProcessor

class DepartmentTagger(DocumentProcessor):
    """Tags each document with the department that owns its source folder."""

    async def process(self, document: Document) -> Document | None:
        if document.source_path is not None:
            document.metadata["department"] = Path(document.source_path).parent.name
        return document

Conventions (see Contributing):

  • Name it *Processor; LLM-based async helpers it delegates to are *Resolvers.
  • Extract reusable logic into standalone functions so it can be tested without the class.
  • Mutating the passed document is fine; returning a new one is too. Return None only to drop it.

Note that extraction is not processing: extractors return typed Mention objects instead of writing to documents — see the Extraction Guide.

docs.title: Rendering
docs.text:
Run interactively: marimo edit docs/notebooks/rendering.py

Rendering converts a Document into a formatted string. ragdoc provides two element renderers and multiple output formats.

docs.title: The two element renderers
docs.text:
Renderer function Intent render_for_prompt Full-fidelity text for LLM context windows and BM25 search render_raw Full fidelity, no transformation — for debugging

render_for_prompt is the primary renderer used throughout the pipeline. It never emits image data: an Image renders as its text_representation, else its alt text, else [Unprocessed Image].

docs.title: Using the Renderer
docs.text:
Renderer combines an element renderer with a target output format:

from ragdoc.rendering import Renderer, render_for_prompt, OutputFormat

# For LLM context windows — full content as Markdown
prompt_renderer = Renderer(
    format=OutputFormat.MARKDOWN,
    element_renderer=render_for_prompt,
)

prompt_text = prompt_renderer.render(document)

docs.title: Output formats
docs.text:
OutputFormat controls the final text format. Element renderers always output HTML internally; the Renderer handles conversion:

Format Description OutputFormat.HTML Raw HTML output (no conversion) OutputFormat.MARKDOWN Standard Markdown OutputFormat.GFM GitHub Flavored Markdown (tables rendered) OutputFormat.RST reStructuredText OutputFormat.PLAIN Plain text (all markup stripped)

MARKDOWN, GFM and RST are converted with pypandoc; HTML is returned as is; PLAIN is the HTML's text content (BeautifulSoup get_text()).

docs.title: Metadata in output
docs.text:
Use metadata_keys to include selected metadata fields as a header in the rendered output:

renderer = Renderer(
    format=OutputFormat.MARKDOWN,
    element_renderer=render_for_prompt,
    metadata_keys=["source", "date", "author"],
    include_title=True,
)
text = renderer.render(document)
# Markdown output starts with a YAML front-matter block (keys sorted, title as a key):
# ---\nauthor: ...\ndate: ...\nsource: ...\ntitle: Document Title\n---\n...content...

docs.title: Inline reference resolution
docs.text:
The Renderer resolves <ref id="..." rel="..."/> tags in element HTML. When a paragraph contains a reference to an image, the renderer replaces the <ref> tag with the rendered content of the image element.

With render_for_prompt, an element that is referenced inline is rendered only at its <ref> location, not a second time as a standalone block. render_raw renders it in both places.

docs.title: Cross-document references
docs.text:
Pass an ExternalRefProvider to make other documents available to custom element renderers (via the render context). The built-in renderers do not use it, so it does not change their output. A plain dict[str, Document] works:

all_docs = {doc.id: doc for doc in all_documents}

renderer = Renderer(
    format=OutputFormat.MARKDOWN,
    element_renderer=render_for_prompt,
    external_refs=all_docs,
)

docs.title: Extending with custom element renderers
docs.text:
Element renderers are singledispatch functions. You can register custom renderers for specific element types:

from ragdoc.rendering.elements import render_for_prompt
from ragdoc.document import Image

@render_for_prompt.register(Image)
def render_image_custom(element, ctx, inline=False):
    alt = element.alt or ""
    return f"<figure><img alt='{alt}'/></figure>"

docs.title: Splitting
docs.text:
Run interactively: marimo edit docs/notebooks/splitting.py

Splitting divides a single Document into multiple smaller documents, each representing a logical section. Splitting is the fourth stage of the pipeline, between processing and chunking.

docs.title: Why split?
docs.text:
LLM context windows and vector store chunks have size limits. Splitting breaks a large document into sections that are:

  • Small enough to fit in a context window
  • Semantically coherent (bounded by headings)
  • Still structured Document objects (not plain text)

Each resulting document carries ExternalRef entries that record the parent-child relationship back to the source document.

docs.title: Split functions
docs.text: ragdoc provides two splitting strategies in ragdoc.splitting:

docs.title: split_by_headings
docs.text:
Splits at every heading boundary, producing a flat list of documents:

from ragdoc.splitting import split_by_headings

sections = split_by_headings(document)
# Each section: one heading + following content, until next heading
# Result: flat list[Document]

Use this when you want uniform granularity — one section per heading regardless of depth.

docs.title: split_hierarchical
docs.text:
Splits once, at the lowest heading level that occurs at least twice; parent headings are prepended to each part as context (split_document applies it recursively):

from ragdoc.splitting import split_hierarchical

sections = split_hierarchical(document)
# Result: list[Document] where each document may contain sub-headings

Use this when you want larger, more self-contained sections that preserve sub-structure.

docs.title: Token-budget splitting: split_document
docs.text:
split_document (what TokenSplitter calls) combines the heading strategies with a token budget. A document that fits is returned as one split; otherwise it is split hierarchically by headings, and sections that still do not fit are packed element by element.

An element that alone exceeds the budget — a 300-row table, a very long list — is cut on its own structural boundaries first:

Element Cut at Each fragment is Table rows (including rows in <tbody> / <tfoot>) a well-formed Table; caption, <colgroup> and header are repeated List items (<dt>/<dd> pairs stay together) a DocumentList; an <ol> continues its numbering via start Other container block children a RawText wrapped in the original outer tag

Fragments keep the outer tag with its attributes and inherit page, bounding_box and metadata; referenced elements (<ref id="…"/>) follow the fragment that contains their reference. Every fragment is measured through the renderer and halved on unit boundaries until it fits. Only a single row or item that is still too large falls through to the text tiers — sentence splitting, then a token slice with overlap_tokens of overlap — which work on rendered text and also verify the rendered result against max_tokens. An element with bare text between its child tags is not cut structurally (the text would be lost); it goes to the text tiers directly.

docs.title: Parent-child relationships
docs.text:
After splitting, each split carries one external-parent entry in external_refs pointing to the source document. The source document is not modified — no external-child entries are written to it; add them yourself if you need them:

sections = split_by_headings(document)

for section in sections:
    parent_refs = [r for r in section.external_refs if r.rel_type == "external-parent"]
    print(f"Section '{section.title}' has parent: {parent_refs}")

A custom element renderer can look related documents up through the renderer's ExternalRefProvider. The built-in renderers do not use it, so these relationships do not change the rendered output by themselves.

docs.title: Post-split processing
docs.text:
Because split results are still Document objects, you can run processors on them after splitting. For example, enrich each section independently with any DocumentProcessor:

from ragdoc.splitting import split_by_headings
from ragdoc.processing import ImageSummaryProcessor
from ragdoc.processing.summary_image import openai_image_summarizer

sections = split_by_headings(document)

processor = ImageSummaryProcessor(summarize=openai_image_summarizer(openai_client))
sections = [await processor.process(section) for section in sections]

docs.title: Reading order
docs.text:
split_document writes metadata["split_sequence"] (1-based position) and metadata["split_total"] (total split count) into every document it produces — including documents that fit within the budget (split_sequence=1, split_total=1). (One gap: a document that is over budget but cannot be split any further comes back as a single split without these keys.) The list it returns is already in reading order, but these keys let you restore that order after documents have been stored, retrieved, or reordered:

splits = split_document(doc, renderer=renderer, max_tokens=5000)

# sorting is a no-op here — splits already in order — but it is safe and explicit:
ordered = sorted(splits, key=lambda d: d.metadata["split_sequence"])

Both keys propagate automatically to Chunk.metadata via the chunker's metadata_fn, so no extra work is needed after chunking.

split_total makes each chunk self-describing: a retrieval client can determine whether the chunk has predecessors (split_sequence > 1) or successors (split_sequence < split_total) without fetching sibling chunks.

split_by_headings, split_hierarchical, and split_by_elements do not set these metadata keys — they are lower-level primitives. Only split_document writes them.

docs.title: Sync Engine
docs.text: Every sync pipeline in ragdoc — VectorStorePipeline, DocumentStorePipeline, and the extraction layer's MentionStorePipeline — is a thin composition over one generic streaming core: SyncEngine[T]. This page explains that shared machinery once; the per-pipeline pages only describe what differs (how sources are resolved and what each source produces).

docs.title: The shape: plan / apply / run
docs.text:
Every sync pipeline exposes the same three methods:

Method What it does Store writes plan(...) Compute a reviewable ChangeSet none apply(changeset) Write a (possibly edited) ChangeSet the whole change set, prepared first, then source by source run(...) Detect changes and write them in one call per source, as produced

run() is a separate streaming path, not a literal apply(plan(...)): when every source succeeds it reaches the same end state — same change detection, same final store contents — but it is scheduled differently.

  • run writes each changed source as soon as it has been produced, so sources written before a later failure stay written. It is back-pressured: a producer keeps its concurrency slot until the writer has taken its result, so at most concurrency + 2 sources' items are held in memory at any time, however large the corpus is. (One lightweight task per source is still created up front.)
  • apply runs the pre_write hook once over the whole change set before it writes anything; for VectorStorePipeline that hook is embedding, so apply embeds all chunks of the change set first. If that fails, the store is untouched and every changed source is reported in errors. Then it deletes the orphans in to_delete and writes the sources one by one. The whole change set is in memory by construction.

apply never mutates the ChangeSet it is given — embedding runs on copies — so a plan still equals its saved copy afterwards, and a saved-then-loaded plan applies exactly like the in-memory one.

Neither path is a transaction across the corpus. After a sync, look at UpdateResult.errors: a source listed there was not (fully) written, and what the store holds for it is described under Write discipline below. One difference between the paths: run() reports every failure there, whereas on the reviewable path a source that fails during hashing or production is left out of the ChangeSet by plan() and only logged (plan(): N source(s) failed …) — apply()'s errors covers embedding and write failures. If embedding fails in apply(), nothing is written and the orphans in to_delete are not deleted either.

docs.title: Human-in-the-loop review
docs.text:
plan() never touches the target store, and its ChangeSet is serializable:

changeset = await pipeline.plan(paths)
changeset.save(Path("review/changes.json"))
# ... inspect / edit the JSON ...
approved = ChangeSet[Chunk].load(Path("review/changes.json"))   # load on the concrete type
result = await pipeline.apply(approved)

A ChangeSet[T] carries to_add / to_update (lists of SourceChange[T] — one entry per changed source with its new items) and to_delete (orphaned source_ids).

docs.title: Change detection: two hashes
docs.text:
Change detection is per source (not per item), keyed on source_id and compared via one of two first-class change tokens:

  • source_hash — SHA-256 of the raw source-file bytes (file_hash). Used on the direct path (Boundary 1): unchanged files are skipped before any parsing or LLM work.
  • content_hash — Document.content_hash(), a canonical-JSON hash over (title, elements) — pure Python, dependency-stable. Used on the Boundary-2 path (reading from a DocumentStore): editing a stored Document's title or elements changes its hash, which triggers re-chunking/re-extraction. A metadata-only edit does not change the hash (metadata, page, bounding_box and provenance fields are excluded), so the stored chunks keep their old metadata until the content changes.

A missing or blank stored hash means "always changed" on either path (None or ""). Stores use that deliberately: a source whose stored items disagree on their hashes, or whose write was interrupted, is reported with blank hashes so it is re-processed.

Both are first-class fields on Chunk and Mention. A Document carries source_hash as a field and computes content_hash() on demand. Neither is ever stored in metadata.

docs.title: The engine, the stores, the producers
docs.text:
SyncEngine[T] owns the invariant machinery:

  • Change detection — compare each source's current token against the stored state (list_source_state()), skip matches.
  • Concurrency — sources are produced under a semaphore (concurrency, an int or a shared asyncio.Semaphore) and streamed as completed. If you share a semaphore, nothing on the write path (the embedder, the store) may acquire that same semaphore: in run the producers hold their slots while they wait for the writer.
  • Error isolation — resolution, production and write failures (Exception subclasses) are caught per source and collected into UpdateResult.errors, so one bad file does not stop the others. Cancellation (asyncio.CancelledError) and other BaseExceptions are not collected; they propagate to the caller, and the running producers are cancelled and awaited before control returns.
  • Write discipline — per source: optional pre_write (embedding), then the write described in the next section.
  • Orphan deletion — sources present in the store but absent upstream are deleted only when delete_orphans=True (opt-in footgun guard: on the direct path, only pass your complete corpus with this flag).

The engine writes to anything satisfying SourceSyncStore[T] — three methods (upsert, delete_by_source, list_source_state) that VectorStore, DocumentStore, and MentionStore all satisfy structurally. A store may additionally implement SourceReplaceStore[T] (replace_source), which changes how updates are written.

docs.title: Write discipline
docs.text:
How a changed source is written depends on what it is and on what the store can do:

Case What the engine calls If the write fails New source upsert(items) Nothing was stored before; the source is re-processed as new next run (assuming the store's upsert does not leave partial items that already carry the final hash) Updated source, store implements SourceReplaceStore replace_source(source_id, items) — new items land before stale ones are removed Store-specific; the contract is that the source must not look "unchanged". The built-in stores are described below: a failure before the stale items are removed leaves the old items in place Updated source, any other store delete_by_source(source_id) then upsert(items) A failed delete skips the upsert (no old/new mixing). A failed upsert leaves the source empty; the next run finds no stored state and re-processes it as new Updated source that now yields no items delete_by_source(source_id) Old items stay; retried next run

pre_write (embedding) runs before any of this, so an embedding failure leaves the store untouched for that source.

The built-in stores that implement SourceReplaceStore are QdrantVectorStore, QdrantMentionStore, QdrantDocumentStore and LocalDocumentStore (LocalMentionStore does not, and its writes are not atomic). A custom store only needs replace_source if it can honour the contract: a failure must not leave the source looking "unchanged", and should leave the previous items in place.

docs.title: What the Qdrant stores guarantee
docs.text:
Qdrant has no multi-request transactions, so the stores make an interrupted write detectable rather than atomic:

  • Blank-then-stamp. A write that spans several requests (more than 100 points, or any replace_source of chunks or mentions) first writes the points with source_hash / content_hash blank and stamps the real hashes with a final set_payload once every batch has landed. Until that stamp, the source reads as "changed". A write that fits one request is a single upsert.
  • A batch of a multi-batch write fails or is cancelled. The points this call created are deleted again, by point id (on cancellation the cleanup runs shielded, then the cancellation is re-raised). Points that existed before the call are never deleted; if the call had already overwritten one, it is not restored to its old content — it keeps the new content with blank hashes. This cleanup covers only the batch-writing phase of a write larger than one batch: a single-request write has no cleanup, and neither has a failure in the later steps below.
  • Replace writes the new points (blank hashes), then deletes only the source's stale points (ids not in the new set), then stamps. What a failure leaves depends on the step: while writing, the old chunks or mentions stay in place (plus the cleanup above for a multi-batch write); at the stale delete, old and new points both remain retrievable, the new ones with blank hashes; at the final stamp, the old points are already gone and the new ones are in place with blank hashes. In every case the source reads as changed and the next sync re-processes it.
  • Hard crash (process killed, power loss). No cleanup runs: the partially written points remain and are retrievable, with blank hashes, so the next sync re-processes the source and replaces them.
  • Mixed state. list_source_state() reports a source whose points disagree on their hashes with blank hashes — "always changed".

QdrantDocumentStore and LocalDocumentStore keep one record per source, so an update is a single atomic replacement (one point; one file written to a temp name and renamed over the old one). A stored document file that cannot be read or parsed is logged and reported as "always changed" instead of aborting the listing: a Boundary-1 re-ingest overwrites it, and at Boundary 2 that one source lands in UpdateResult.errors while the others proceed.

docs.title: Two things that are not guarantees
docs.text:
• A source that yields no items is re-produced on every run. The change token lives on the stored items; with nothing stored there is nothing to compare against, so the source is parsed, processed and (where applicable) sent to the LLM again each time until it yields items.
  • A processor-filtered document is treated differently by the direct paths. DocumentStorePipeline keeps the previously stored Document (the producer returns None); VectorStorePipeline and MentionStorePipeline in direct mode delete the source's stored chunks / mentions (the producer returns an empty change) and count the source as processed. This is current behaviour, not a contract of the engine.

What each pipeline contributes is just:

  1. Resolution — turning its request (file paths, or source_ids in a DocumentStore) into a SyncPlanInput: the sources to evaluate, each with its current change token, plus the reference set for orphan comparison.
  2. A producer — one coroutine SyncSource -> SourceChange[T] | None that materializes a changed source's new items: parse+process+chunk (VectorStorePipeline), parse+process (DocumentStorePipeline), or split+extract (MentionStorePipeline). Returning an empty item list means "this source now yields nothing" (its stale entries are deleted); returning None means "unavailable" (warned + counted as skipped). DocumentStorePipeline returns None when processing filters a document out, so a transient filter (or a misclassifying LLM processor) never deletes the previously stored copy. Resolution failures (an unreadable or vanished file during hashing) are captured per path instead of aborting the run: they surface in UpdateResult.errors and the affected source is never treated as an orphan.

docs.title: How the three pipelines compose it
docs.text:
Pipeline Boundary Change token Producer Sink DocumentStorePipeline(ingest=…) 1 source_hash IngestPipeline.run (parse → process) DocumentStore VectorStorePipeline(pipeline=…) direct source_hash full DocumentPipeline.run (parse → … → chunk) VectorStore VectorStorePipeline.from_document_store(chunk=…) 2 content_hash ChunkPipeline.run on stored Documents VectorStore MentionStorePipeline(ingest=…) direct source_hash ingest → split → Extractor.extract MentionStore MentionStorePipeline.from_document_store(…) 2 content_hash split → extract on stored Documents MentionStore

Each pipeline takes the boundary-appropriate pipeline type (IngestPipeline or ChunkPipeline). Those types have no parameter for a stage from the other side (IngestPipeline(splitter=…) is a TypeError), so a misplaced stage cannot be expressed. The sync pipelines do not check the class of the pipeline object at runtime, though — passing, say, a DocumentPipeline where an IngestPipeline is expected is caught by a type checker, not at construction. See the Pipeline Guide for the two-stage workflow.

docs.title: Result accounting
docs.text:
All three return the same UpdateResult, keyed on source_id:

result = await pipeline.run(paths)
result.processed   # newly added or updated (also: a source that now yields nothing, its items deleted)
result.skipped     # change token matched (or source unavailable)
result.deleted     # orphans removed (only with delete_orphans=True)
result.errors      # [(source_id, exception)] — isolated per source

docs.title: Extending: your own synced sink
docs.text: Point the engine at a new sink by implementing the three SourceSyncStore methods and writing a producer — no engine changes. Add replace_source (see Write discipline) if your backend can write a source's new items before removing the old ones. Index your backing store on the item's source_id field (a first-class field, not metadata) so delete_by_source and list_source_state stay cheap; see Implementing a custom VectorStore for a concrete example.
